title: Edge Length, Surface Area, and Volume of a Cube from Its Space Diagonal
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Express the edge length x of a cube as a function of the cube's space diagonal length d. Then express the total surface area A and volume V of the cube as functions of d.

steps.title: Relate Edge Length x to Space Diagonal d
steps.mathExpression: x^2 + x^2 + x^2 = d^2 \implies 3x^2 = d^2 \implies x(d) = \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}}
steps.explanation: A face diagonal of a cube of edge x has length sqrt(x^2 + x^2) = sqrt(2)x. Applying the Pythagorean theorem to the right triangle formed by an edge x, a face diagonal sqrt(2)x, and the space diagonal d gives 3x^2 = d^2, so x = d / sqrt(3).
steps.why: By the three-dimensional Pythagorean theorem, the squared space diagonal of a rectangular box equals the sum of the squares of its three orthogonal dimensions.

steps.title: Express the Surface Area A as a Function of d
steps.explanation: A cube has 6 congruent square faces, each of area x^2. Substituting x^2 = d^2 / 3 into A = 6x^2 simplifies to A(d) = 2d^2.
steps.why: Total surface area is the sum of the areas of all six square faces.

steps.title: Express the Volume V as a Function of d
steps.explanation: The volume of a cube of edge x is V = x^3. Substituting x = d / sqrt(3) and cubing numerator and denominator yields V(d) = d^3 / (3*sqrt(3)).
steps.why: Cubing a quotient raises both the numerator and denominator to the third power, with (sqrt(3))^3 = 3*sqrt(3).
